clue.text: Pauses in Hamlet upsetting

indicators.note: the answer sits in the words that follow

blocks.note: the last three letters of the play's name and the first three of the next word

explanation.surface: A critic complains that the pauses spoil a performance of Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Hamlet look like the play under review, but only its last three letters matter; 'upsetting' reads like a reversal signal and is just more fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a let-up is a lull or easing off, a brief stop in something that then carries on.

clue.text: One magazine, then another: you’re here for it all!

definitions.note: a cryptic, whole-phrase description of the noun: the span you are alive for

explanation.surface: A newsagent's cheery pitch to a customer browsing magazine after magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: the only span you are present for from start to finish is your own.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the whole stretch between birth and death is the one period every person attends in full.

clue.text: It’s decrepit?

indicators.note: worn out and falling apart, so the letters of ITS are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone asks, perhaps of a wobbly old chair, whether it is past its best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' does double duty: its letters are the fodder, and the answer is the old-fashioned contraction of it is, suitably decrepit itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic form: poets and old plays shorten 'it is' this way, with the apostrophe at the front instead.

clue.text: Red / green / yellow ingredient topping Italy’s pizza’s … topping!

blocks.note: bell peppers come red, green or yellow
on = on top of; in a down clue the vegetable sits on the I
I = Italy, its international vehicle code

explanation.surface: A menu line listing pizza toppings, the colours of the peppers split by slashes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' appears twice on purpose: the first is the positional ON, the second belongs to the definition, pizza's classic topping.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the spicy Italian-American sausage, sliced thin, is the most popular thing scattered over a pizza.

clue.text: As these words are like most poetry

blocks.note: the words are printed in italics, so emphasised
most verse has a regular metre of strong and weak syllables

explanation.surface: A remark on poetic style, comparing the clue's own words to verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition only works in print: italics are how a writer marks emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic type shows emphasis on words, and metrical verse puts emphasis on syllables in a regular beat.

clue.text: Article on public land leading to Parky’s indisposition

blocks.note: an area of land open to all local people
'parky' is British slang for chilly; Parky's = parky is

explanation.surface: A story about a walk across a public common that left Parky under the weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Parky was the nickname of TV interviewer Michael Parkinson, so the name looks like a person; as a plain word, parky is British slang for chilly, and the 's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a runny nose and sore throat from a virus is the most familiar minor ailment there is.

clue.text: Casts Cockney as gentry

definitions.note: gentry is a collective noun; the answer is a plural of its members

indicators.note: a Cockney drops the H, so HURLS is said 'URLS

blocks.note: casts = hurls; with a Cockney's dropped H it is 'urls

explanation.surface: A theatre director casts a Cockney actor to play the aristocrats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casts' pulls towards actors and parts, but it is the throwing kind: hurls.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose sense: strictly the gentry sit just below the peerage, but the word is used for titled, landed people generally.

clue.text: Young man with gloom lifting snogs wildly in erotic verse

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting turns FOG upwards to read GOF
the letters of SNOGS run wild

explanation.surface: A moody youth kissing passionately, as if in a steamy poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Snog is British slang for a passionate kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament book also called the Song of Solomon is a sequence of sensual love poems between two lovers.

clue.text: Primarily, decidedly ritzy / elegantly styled – suit yourself!

definitions.text: Primarily, decidedly ritzy / elegantly styled – suit yourself!

indicators.note: take the first letter of each following word

blocks.clueFragment: decidedly ritzy / elegantly styled – suit yourself

explanation.surface: A dress code note: aim for smart and glamorous, but interpret it as you like.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: its words describe smart clothes, and their initials spell it.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes clothing that is glamorous and smart, worn for an occasion, which is what the adjective means.

clue.text: Perhaps Sturgeon’s gone east for pescatarian option

blocks.note: a sturgeon is a fish, 'perhaps' marking the example

explanation.surface: A political story: Nicola Sturgeon, the former Scottish First Minister, has headed east.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S dresses the fish up as the politician. Fish paste is a British sandwich spread.
explanation.definitionFit: A pescatarian eats seafood but no meat, so a spread made from ground fish is something they can choose.

clue.text: Film rebooted: I Took The Limes

indicators.note: restarted in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A film remake announced under a new, rather odd title.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals and italics dress the fodder up as a film title, which fits the movie reboot of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the 1959 Billy Wilder comedy starring Marilyn Monroe, Tony Curtis and Jack Lemmon.

clue.text: Stray found in mountains

explanation.surface: A lost animal turns up in the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' looks like a noun, a lost dog, but it is the verb: to wander.
explanation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms: cattle wander widely over open country, and a line of connected peaks shares the same name.

clue.text: Follow edges of footprint?

blocks.note: draw round an outline, as with tracing paper

explanation.surface: Drawing round a footprint, as a detective or a child might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edges of' looks like an instruction to take the outer letters of footprint, but it belongs to the first definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Copying an outline through thin paper is one sense; a faint mark or sign that someone passed is the other.

clue.text: Fancy lady revamping sad churches

indicators.note: remaking something, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A wealthy woman pays to restore run-down churches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an anagram signal but it belongs to the definition: a very grand lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful definition: a woman of Habsburg imperial rank is about as grand and titled as nobility gets.

clue.text: Lowers trousers, having consumed liquor: high-risk actions

indicators.note: MOONS swallows SHOT, which goes inside

blocks.note: to bare one's bottom as a prank

explanation.surface: Someone drops their trousers after a few drinks, a risky thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a drunken prank, and the drink really does end up inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after launching rockets at our satellite, the word now covers any ambitious venture that may well fail.

clue.text: Critical memos rewritten; they only cover small areas

indicators.note: written again in a new order

explanation.surface: Office memos that got redrafted and ended up narrow in scope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests paperwork's remit, but here it is weather conditions over a patch of ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Local weather patterns, such as in a sheltered valley or walled garden, differ from the surrounding region's.

clue.text: Delicious quality: after time, wine going to head

indicators.note: after means coming later in sequence, so the wine is written following the letter for time

blocks.note: a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: After a while, a delicious wine starts going to your head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' reads as the drinker's head, but it is a promontory.
explanation.definitionFit: The abstract noun for food that has lots of flavour and is pleasant to eat.

clue.text: Rates fools, storing jam with no lid

indicators.note: to store something is to keep it inside, so the fools hold the jam's remaining letters within them
in a down clue the lid is the top letter, so MESS loses its M

blocks.note: jam = mess (a fix), minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A cook judges fools, the fruit puddings, while putting away jars of jam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fools' and 'jam' suggest the kitchen (a fool is a fruit dessert), but a jam here is a tight spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to evaluate or judge the worth or quality of something.

clue.text: Greatly enjoy percussion overwhelming Sweden’s rowdy music

indicators.note: to overwhelm is to engulf or bury, so the percussion closes around Sweden's letter

blocks.note: to drink in = to savour eagerly
metal discs struck with a beater
S = Sweden, its international vehicle code

explanation.surface: Loud drums drowning out Swedish music at a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: The break between the two words falls in a different place from the parse: DRINK IN + G(S)ONGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunes bellowed together in pubs and beer halls, usually loud and boisterous.

clue.text: Passed over – lamented

explanation.surface: A euphemism for dying, 'passed over', followed by the mourning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed over' suggests death, which fits 'lamented', but it means skipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one verb: failing to take an opportunity, and wishing an absent person were still around.

clue.text: At home with insignificant type, idiot, nothing, no-name

blocks.note: a small cog in the machine

explanation.surface: A string of insults for a nobody sitting at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a pile-up of put-downs; the last one is the definition, used as an adjective: unnamed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone travelling under a false identity conceals who they are, so goes about without their real label.

clue.text: Creep up on a policeman in Limerick

indicators.note: in a down clue, up turns DRAG over to read GARD

explanation.surface: Advice on sneaking up on an Irish police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Limerick is an Irish city, not the comic verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish word for guard names both the Republic's police force and an individual officer in it.

clue.text: Send out one’s children

explanation.surface: A parent packing the kids off out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one action, but the dash-free split falls after 'out'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: releasing stamps or statements officially, and the formal legal term for a person's descendants.

clue.text: Cut – or pure, you say?

indicators.note: the answer is what 'sheer' sounds like when spoken

explanation.surface: Someone checking whether a fabric is cut or pure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' offers the two words as alternatives; they sound alike and differ in spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: clipping wool from sheep, or slicing metal with blades.

clue.text: Stalls accommodating greedy-guts, prickly types

indicators.note: HEDGES makes room for HOG inside

blocks.note: to stall = to avoid committing, evade

explanation.surface: Market stalls, or theatre seats, full of greedy people with spiky tempers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalls' reads as a noun, but it is the verb: dodges.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun: the small spiny mammals are literally covered in prickles, while the phrase usually means touchy people.

clue.text: Everyman? Joke

blocks.note: any person at all, the impersonal pronoun
as in 'have you heard the … about'

explanation.walkthrough: The setter names the crossword itself: Everyman is the puzzle's pen name, and an everyman is anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: The impersonal pronoun stands for any person, and a told gag is 'a good one'.

clue.text: Aversion: staidest upset

indicators.note: knocked over, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: The most prim people are upset by something they dislike.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a reaction to prudes being offended, which fits the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a feeling of dislike or mild disgust towards something.

clue.text: Guides some of gnus herself

indicators.note: only part of the following letters is used

blocks.note: the tail of the first word and the head of the second

explanation.surface: A wildlife guide leads some of the gnu herd on her own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guides' looks like a noun for safari leaders, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: people who lead guests to their seats at weddings, theatres and cinemas do exactly this.
